[61911] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 tit. 2 Et videtur quod non.

[61912] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 1 Dicitur enim Eccli. XV, 18: ante hominem vita et mors, bonum et malum: quodcumque voluerit, dabitur ei. Ex quo potest accipi, quod peccatum, quod est spiritualis mors animae, in voluntate consistit. Sed nihil quod homo contrahit ex origine sua, consistit in eius voluntate. Ergo nullum peccatum contrahit homo ex sua origine.

[61913] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 2 Praeterea, accidens non traducitur nisi per traductionem sui subiecti. Subiectum autem peccati est anima rationalis. Cum ergo anima rationalis non traducatur per originem, ut habetur in Lib. de Eccl. dogmatibus, videtur quod neque aliquod peccatum per originem contrahatur.

[61914] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 3 Sed dicendum, quod licet subiectum peccati non traducatur, traducitur tamen caro, quae est causa peccati.- Sed contra, ad traductionem accidentis non sufficit traductio eius quod non est sufficiens causa; quia ea posita, non ponitur effectus. Sed caro non est sufficiens causa peccati; quia quantumcumque caro alliciat ad peccandum, in potestate tamen voluntatis est assentire vel non assentire; et sic ipsa voluntas est sufficiens causa peccati. Sed voluntas non traducitur. Ergo traductio carnis non sufficit ad traductionem alicuius peccati.

[61915] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 4 Praeterea, peccatum, secundum quod nunc accipitur, est cui debetur poena et increpatio. Sed nulli defectui ex origine contracto debetur increpatio et poena: sicut enim dicit philosophus in III Ethic., si quis est caecus ex infirmitate, non increpatur; increpatur autem si sit caecus ex ebrietate. Ergo nullus defectus qui ex origine contrahitur, habet rationem peccati.

[61916] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 5 Praeterea, Augustinus in I de libero arbitrio distinguit duplex malum: unum quod agimus, quod est malum culpae, et aliud quod patimur, quod pertinet ad malum poenae. Sed omnis defectus qui est ex alio, habet rationem passionis; nam passio est effectus illatioque actionis. Ergo nihil quod contrahitur per originem ex alio habet rationem peccati, sed solum rationem poenae.

[61917] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 6 Praeterea, in Lib. de ecclesiasticis dogmatibus dicitur: bona est caro nostra, utpote a bono Deo creata. Sed bonum non est causa mali, secundum illud Matth. VII, 18: non potest arbor bona fructus malos facere. Ergo peccatum originale non contrahitur per carnis originem.

[61918] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 7 Praeterea, plus dependet anima a carne postquam ei est unita, quam in ipsa eius unitione. Sed postquam anima iam est carni unita, non potest infici a carne nisi per suum consensum. Ergo neque in ipsa unitione. Peccatum ergo originale non potest contrahi per carnis originem.

[61919] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 8 Praeterea, si origo carnis vitiata peccatum causat in anima, quanto origo fuerit magis vitiata, tanto maius peccatum causabit. Sed in illis qui nascuntur ex fornicatione, magis est vitiata origo quam in illis qui nascuntur ex legitimo matrimonio. Sequeretur ergo quod illi qui ex fornicatione nascuntur, maius peccatum contrahant nascendo; quod patet esse falsum: quia non debetur eis maior poena.

[61920] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 9 Praeterea, si peccatum originale contrahitur per carnis originem, hoc non est nisi in quantum caro est corrupta. Aut ergo illa corruptio est moralis, aut naturalis. Sed moralis esse non potest: quia corruptionis moralis subiectum non est caro, sed anima. Similiter autem nec naturalis: quia sequeretur quod inficeret animam naturali actione, id est per qualitates activas et passivas; quod patet esse falsum. Nullo ergo modo peccatum contrahitur per carnis originem.

[61921] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 10 Praeterea, defectus qui consecutus est ex peccato primi parentis, est carentia originalis iustitiae, ut Anselmus dicit; et sic cum originalis iustitia sit quiddam spirituale, sequitur quod defectus praedictus sit etiam spiritualis. Corruptio autem carnis est quiddam corporale. Spiritualia autem et corporalia sunt diversorum generum; et sic spirituale non potest causare effectum corporalem. Non ergo ex peccato primi parentis potuit causari corruptio in carne nostra, ex qua in nobis peccatum per originem transfunderetur.

[61922] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 11 Praeterea, secundum Augustinum, peccatum originale est carentia originalis iustitiae. Aut ergo originalis iustitia conveniebat animae primi hominis naturaliter ex sua creatione, aut fuit donum superadditum ex divina liberalitate. Si autem fuit animae naturalis, nunquam eam amisisset peccando: quia, ut Dionysius dicit IV cap. de Div. Nom., data naturalia etiam in Daemonibus permanserunt; et sic etiam omnes homines originalem iustitiam haberent: quia quod est naturale uni animae, est omnibus animabus naturale; et ita nullus nasceretur cum peccato originali, idest cum carentia originalis iustitiae. Si autem fuit iustitia illa donum superadditum ex liberalitate divina: aut ergo Deus animae hominis nascentis illud donum dat, aut non. Si dat, non nascitur homo cum carentia originalis iustitiae, neque potest anima eius per carnem infici. Si autem non datur a Deo, hoc non videtur ei esse imputandum, sed Deo, qui non dedit. Nullo ergo modo homo per originem peccatum contrahere potest.

[61923] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 12 Praeterea, anima rationalis non supervenit alicui formae praeexistenti: quia non adveniret materiae tamquam forma substantialis, sed tamquam materia accidentalis, quae advenit subiecto iam existenti in actu. Oportet ergo quod adveniente anima rationali, deficiant omnes formae praeexistentes, et per consequens omnia accidentia. Cessat ergo et ipsa corruptio seminis, si qua inerat a generante. Non ergo anima adveniens per carnem inquinari potest.

[61924] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 13 Praeterea, motus sequitur naturam elementi praedominantis in corporibus mixtis, et per consequens omnes proprietates consequuntur illud quod praedominatur in composito. Sed anima praedominatur corpori in homine, qui ex utroque componitur; anima autem ex sua origine habet puritatem. Licet ergo caro ex sua origine aliquam impuritatem contrahat, videtur tamen quod homo nascens non debeat dici infectus peccato, sed purus.

[61925] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 14 Praeterea, peccatum est cui aliqua poena debetur: sed peccato quod per originem contrahitur, non debetur aliqua poena; nam carentia visionis divinae, quae communiter assignatur ei pro poena, non videtur esse aliqua poena; quia si homo moreretur absque omni peccato, et gratiam non haberet, non posset pervenire ad visionem divinam, in qua consistit vita aeterna, secundum illud Ioan. XVII, v. 3: haec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum; et apostolus dicit, Rom. VI, 23: gratia Dei vita aeterna. Non ergo est aliquod peccatum quod per originem contrahatur.

[61926] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 15 Praeterea, sicut causa prima est nobilior quam secunda, ita causa secunda est nobilior quam effectus. Sed si peccatum traducitur a primo parente, corruptio consecuta est in carne per animam primi hominis peccantis, et ex carne perducitur ad animam hominis qui nascitur ex Adam; et sic anima primi hominis est sicut causa prima, caro autem sicut causa secunda, et anima hominis generati sicut effectus ultimus. Sic ergo anima primi hominis erit nobilior, et caro nobilior quam anima hominis generati; quod est inconveniens. Non ergo peccatum potest traduci per originem.

[61927] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 16 Praeterea, nihil agit nisi in quantum est actu. Sed in semine non est actu peccatum. Non ergo per semen decisum anima infici potest aliquo peccato.

[61928] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 17 Praeterea, non potest esse idem causa infectionis peccati, et meriti. Sed actus generationis aliquando potest esse meritorius; puta cum aliquis in gratia existens, ad uxorem accedit causa generandae prolis, vel debiti reddendi. Non ergo ex hoc poterit causari infectio peccati in prole.

[61929] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 18 Praeterea, causa particularis non inducit effectum universalem. Sed peccatum Adae fuit quoddam particulare. Non ergo potuit inficere totam humanam naturam aliquo peccato.

[61930] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 19 Praeterea, dominus dicit Ezech. XVIII, v. 4: omnes animae meae sunt; et vers. 30: filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. Portaret autem, si pro peccato primi hominis hi qui ab eo nascuntur, damnarentur. Non ergo peccatum in posteros Adae traducitur propter eius peccatum.

[61931] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. 1 Sed contra. Est quod dicitur, Rom. V, v. 12: per unum hominem peccatum in hunc mundum intravit. Sed non per imitationem; quia sic per Diabolum peccatum in mundum intravit, secundum illud Sap. II, 24-25: invidia Diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum. Imitantur autem illum qui sunt ex parte eius. Ergo per originem vitiatam peccatum a primo homine in posteros derivatur.

[61932] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. 2 Praeterea, Augustinus dicit XIV de civitate Dei quod primus homo sponte depravatus genuit filios depravatos. Sed depravatio non fit nisi per peccatum. Ergo filii Adam ex sua origine peccatum contrahunt.

[61933] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 co. Respondeo. Dicendum quod Pelagiani negaverunt aliquod peccatum per originem posse traduci. Sed hoc ex magna parte excludit necessitatem redemptionis factae per Christum, quae maxime videtur necessaria fuisse ad abolendam infectionem peccati, quae a primo parente in totam eius posteritatem derivata est, dicente apostolo, Rom. V, 18, quod sicut per unius delictum processum est in omnes homines in condemnationem, sic et per unius iustitiam in omnes homines in iustificationem vitae. Excluditur etiam necessitas pueros baptizandi, quod tamen communis Ecclesiae consuetudo habet ab apostolis derivata, ut Dionysius dicit in ecclesiastica Hierar. Et ideo simpliciter dicendum est, quod peccatum traducitur per originem a primo parente in posteros. Ad cuius evidentiam considerandum est, quod aliquis homo singularis dupliciter potest considerari: uno modo secundum quod est quaedam persona singularis; alio modo secundum quod est pars alicuius collegii, et utroque modo ad eum potest aliquis actus pertinere. Pertinet enim ad eum in quantum est singularis persona, ille actus quem proprio arbitrio et per se ipsum facit; sed in quantum est pars collegii, potest ad eum pertinere actus aliquis quem per se ipsum non facit nec proprio arbitrio, sed qui fit a toto collegio vel a pluribus de collegio vel a principe collegii; sicut illud quod princeps civitatis facit, dicitur civitas facere, ut philosophus dicit. Huiusmodi enim collegium hominum reputatur quasi unus homo, ita quod diversi homines in diversis officiis constituti sunt quasi diversa membra unius corporis naturalis, ut apostolus inducit de membris Ecclesiae, I Cor. XII, 12. Sic ergo tota multitudo hominum a primo parente humanam naturam accipientium, quasi unum collegium, vel potius sicut unum corpus unius hominis consideranda est; in qua quidem multitudo unusquisque homo, etiam ipse Adam, potest considerari vel quasi singularis persona, vel quasi aliquod membrum huius multitudinis, quae per naturalem originem derivatur ab uno. Est autem considerandum quod primo homini in sua institutione datum fuerat divinitus quoddam supernaturale donum, scilicet originalis iustitia, per quam ratio subdebatur Deo, et inferiores vires rationi, et corpus animae. Hoc autem donum non fuerat datum primo homini ut singulari personae tantum, sed ut cuidam principio totius humanae naturae, ut scilicet ab eo per originem derivaretur in posteros. Hoc autem donum acceptum primus homo per liberum arbitrium peccans amisit eo tenore quo sibi datum fuerat, scilicet pro se et pro tota sua posteritate. Defectus ergo huius doni totam eius posteritatem consequitur; et sic iste defectus eo modo traducitur in posteros quo modo traducitur humana natura; quae quidem traducitur non quidem secundum se totam, sed secundum aliquam sui partem, scilicet secundum carnem, cui Deus animam infundit; et sic sicut anima divinitus infusa pertinet ad naturam humanam ab Adam derivatam, propter carnem cui coniungitur; ita et defectus praedictus pertinet ad animam propter carnem, quae ab Adam propagatur non solum secundum corpulentam substantiam, sed etiam secundum seminalem rationem, id est non solum materialiter, sed sicut ab activo principio: sic enim filius accipit a patre naturam humanam. Si ergo consideretur iste defectus hoc modo per originem in istum hominem derivatus, secundum illud quod iste homo est quaedam persona singularis, sic huiusmodi defectus, non potest habere rationem culpae, ad cuius rationem requiritur quod sit voluntaria. Sed si consideretur iste homo generatus sicut quoddam membrum totius humanae naturae a primo parente propagatae, ac si omnes homines essent unus homo, sic habet rationem culpae propter voluntarium eius principium, quod est actuale peccatum primi parentis; sicut si dicamus, quod motus manus ad homicidium perpetrandum, secundum quod manus per se consideratur, non habet rationem culpae, quia manus de necessitate movetur ab alio. Si autem consideretur ut est pars totius hominis, qui voluntate agit, sic habet rationem culpae, quia sic est voluntarius. Sicut ergo homicidium non dicitur culpa manus, sed culpa totius hominis; ita huiusmodi defectus non dicitur esse peccatum personale, sed peccatum totius naturae; nec ad personam pertinet, nisi in quantum natura inficit personam. Et sicut ad unum peccatum faciendum diversae partes hominis adhibentur, scilicet voluntas, ratio, manus et huiusmodi, et tamen est unum solum peccatum propter unitatem principii, scilicet voluntatis, a quo peccati ratio ad omnes actus partium derivatur; ita et ratione principii in tota natura humana consideratur quasi unum peccatum originale; propter quod apostolus dicit, Rom. V, 12: in quo omnes peccaverunt; quod secundum Augustinum, potest intelligi in quo scilicet primo homine, vel in quo peccato primi hominis, ut peccatum primi hominis sit quasi commune peccatum omnium.

[61934] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 1 Ad primum ergo dicendum, quod peccatum quod per originem contrahitur, dicitur voluntarium ratione sui principii, scilicet voluntatis primi parentis, ut dictum est.

[61935] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 2 Ad secundum dicendum, quod istud peccatum consequitur totam naturam humanam; unde subiectum huius peccati est anima, secundum quod est pars humanae naturae: et ideo sicut humana natura traducitur, licet anima non traducatur; ita etiam peccatum originale traducitur, licet anima non traducatur.

[61936] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 3 Ad tertium dicendum, quod caro non est sufficiens causa peccati actualis, sed peccati originalis est sufficiens causa; sicut et traductio carnis est sufficiens causa, materialiter tamen, humanae naturae.

[61937] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 4 Ad quartum dicendum, quod ei quod est per originem contractum, non debetur poena et increpatio si referatur ad personam, quia sic non habet rationem voluntarii, sed si referatur ad naturam, sic habet rationem voluntarii, ut dictum est et hoc modo debetur ei increpatio et poena.

[61938] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 5 Ad quintum dicendum, quod defectus per originem contractus habet quidem rationem existentis ab alio, si referatur ad personam, non autem si referatur ad naturam; sic enim est quasi a principio intrinseco.

[61939] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 6 Ad sextum dicendum, quod caro nostra in sui natura bona est, sed secundum quod est privata originali iustitia propter peccatum primi parentis, sic causat originale peccatum.

[61940] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 7 Ad septimum dicendum, quod sicut dictum est, peccatum originale per se loquendo est peccatum naturae, non personae, nisi ratione naturae infectae. Actus autem generationis proprie deservit naturae, quia ordinatur ad conservationem speciei; sed carnem iam esse animae unitam pertinet ad constitutionem personae; et ideo caro magis causat originale peccatum prout consideratur in via generationis quam prout est iam unita.

[61941] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 8 Ad octavum dicendum, quod in illis qui nascuntur ex fornicatione, est quidem origo dupliciter vitiata, vitio scilicet naturae, quod traducitur ex Adam, et vitio personae, id est patris generantis, ex quo vitio nulla infectio in prole relinquitur. Quilibet enim generans traducit peccatum originale in quantum generat ut Adam, non in quantum generat ut Petrus vel Martinus; id est per id quod habet ab Adam, non per id quod est proprium sibi.

[61942] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 9 Ad nonum dicendum, quod corruptio quae est in carne, est quidem actus naturalis, sed intentione et virtute moralis. Ex peccato enim primi parentis destituta est caro eius illa virtute ut ex ea possit decidi semen per quod originalis iustitia in alios propagetur; et sic in semine defectus huius virtutis est defectus moralis corruptionis, et quaedam intentio eius; sicut dicimus intentionem coloris esse in aere, et intentionem animae esse in semine. Et ex hoc etiam est ibi virtus ad similem imperfectionem, sicut est ibi virtus ad productionem humanae naturae in prole generata.

[61943] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 10 Ad decimum dicendum, quod nihil prohibet a causa spirituali causari effectum corporalem. Nam et Boetius dicit in libro de Trinitate quod formae quae sunt in materia, venerunt a formis quae sunt sine materia: et in nobis ipsis a voluntate movetur inferior appetitus, ad cuius motum sequitur transmutatio corporalis.

[61944] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 11 Ad undecimum dicendum, quod originalis iustitia fuit superaddita primo homini ex liberalitate divina; sed quod huic animae non detur a Deo, non est ex parte eius, sed ex parte humanae naturae, in qua invenitur contrarium prohibens.

[61945] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 12 Ad duodecimum dicendum, quod in semine est corruptio originalis peccati non actu sed virtute, eo modo quo est ibi virtute humana natura: quae quidem virtus activa in semine est in spiritu spumoso, ut Aristoteles dicit in Lib. de Gener. animalium, non autem in materia quae amittit unam formam et recipit aliam.

[61946] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 13 Ad decimumtertium dicendum, quod sicut Dionysius dicit IV cap. de Div. Nom., bonum contingit ex tota integra causa, sed malum provenit etiam ex singularibus defectibus; et ideo defectus qui est ex parte corporis sufficit ad integritatem humanae naturae tollendam.

[61947] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 14 Ad decimumquartum dicendum, quod carentia divinae visionis dupliciter competit alicui. Uno modo sic quod non habeat in se unde possit ad divinam visionem pervenire, et sic carentia divinae visionis competeret ei qui in solis naturalibus esset etiam absque peccato; sic enim carentia divinae visionis non est poena, sed defectus consequens omnem naturam creatam: quia nulla creatura ex suis naturalibus potest pervenire ad visionem divinam. Alio modo potest alicui competere carentia divinae visionis hoc modo ut habeat in se aliquid ex quo debeatur ei quod careat visione divina; et sic carentia visionis divinae est poena et originalis et actualis peccati.

[61948] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 15 Ad decimumquintum dicendum, quod duplex est causa. Una principalis quae agit per propriam formam, et haec est nobilior quam effectus in quantum est causa. Alia est causa instrumentalis quae non agit per formam propriam, sed in quantum est mota ab alio, et hanc non oportet nobiliorem esse effectu, sicut serra non est nobilior quam domus. Hoc autem modo semen carnale est causa naturae humanae in prole, et etiam culpae originalis in anima eius.

[61949] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 16 Ad decimumsextum dicendum, quod aliquod agens est in actu multipliciter. Uno modo secundum propriam formam, quae vel continet formam effectus secundum similitudinem speciei, sicut ignis generat ignem; vel secundum virtutem tantum, sicut sol generat ignem. Alio modo, secundum motum ab alio; et hoc modo instrumentum agit ut ens actu: et sic etiam semen est actu, in quantum est in eo motus et intentio animae generantis, secundum philosophum in Lib. de Gener. animalium; et ex hoc habet virtutem causandi et humanam naturam et originale peccatum.

[61950] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 17 Ad decimumseptimum dicendum, quod aliquis vir iustus accedendo ad uxorem meretur secundum id quod est proprium sibi; et sic non transmittit peccatum originale, sed secundum id quod habet ab Adam, ut supra dictum est.

[61951] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 18 Ad decimumoctavum dicendum, quod Adam in quantum fuit principium humanae naturae, habuit rationem causae universalis, et ita per eius actum corrupta est tota humana natura, quae ab eo propagatur.

[61952] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 19 Ad decimumnonum dicendum, quod peccatum primi hominis est quodammodo peccatum commune totius humanae naturae, ut dictum est; et ideo cum aliquis punitur pro peccato primi parentis, non punitur pro peccato alterius, sed pro peccato suo.
la.text: [61911] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 tit. 2 Et videtur quod non. [61912] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 1 Dicitur enim Eccli. XV, 18: ante hominem vita et mors, bonum et malum: quodcumque voluerit, dabitur ei. Ex quo potest accipi, quod peccatum, quod est spiritualis mors animae, in voluntate consistit. Sed nihil quod homo contrahit ex origine sua, consistit in eius voluntate. Ergo nullum peccatum contrahit homo ex sua origine. [61913] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 2 Praeterea, accidens non traducitur nisi per traductionem sui subiecti. Subiectum autem peccati est anima rationalis. Cum ergo anima rationalis non traducatur per originem, ut habetur in Lib. de Eccl. dogmatibus, videtur quod neque aliquod peccatum per originem contrahatur. [61914] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 3 Sed dicendum, quod licet subiectum peccati non traducatur, traducitur tamen caro, quae est causa peccati.- Sed contra, ad traductionem accidentis non sufficit traductio eius quod non est sufficiens causa; quia ea posita, non ponitur effectus. Sed caro non est sufficiens causa peccati; quia quantumcumque caro alliciat ad peccandum, in potestate tamen voluntatis est assentire vel non assentire; et sic ipsa voluntas est sufficiens causa peccati. Sed voluntas non traducitur. Ergo traductio carnis non sufficit ad traductionem alicuius peccati. [61915] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 4 Praeterea, peccatum, secundum quod nunc accipitur, est cui debetur poena et increpatio. Sed nulli defectui ex origine contracto debetur increpatio et poena: sicut enim dicit philosophus in III Ethic., si quis est caecus ex infirmitate, non increpatur; increpatur autem si sit caecus ex ebrietate. Ergo nullus defectus qui ex origine contrahitur, habet rationem peccati. [61916] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 5 Praeterea, Augustinus in I de libero arbitrio distinguit duplex malum: unum quod agimus, quod est malum culpae, et aliud quod patimur, quod pertinet ad malum poenae. Sed omnis defectus qui est ex alio, habet rationem passionis; nam passio est effectus illatioque actionis. Ergo nihil quod contrahitur per originem ex alio habet rationem peccati, sed solum rationem poenae. [61917] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 6 Praeterea, in Lib. de ecclesiasticis dogmatibus dicitur: bona est caro nostra, utpote a bono Deo creata. Sed bonum non est causa mali, secundum illud Matth. VII, 18: non potest arbor bona fructus malos facere. Ergo peccatum originale non contrahitur per carnis originem. [61918] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 7 Praeterea, plus dependet anima a carne postquam ei est unita, quam in ipsa eius unitione. Sed postquam anima iam est carni unita, non potest infici a carne nisi per suum consensum. Ergo neque in ipsa unitione. Peccatum ergo originale non potest contrahi per carnis originem. [61919] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 8 Praeterea, si origo carnis vitiata peccatum causat in anima, quanto origo fuerit magis vitiata, tanto maius peccatum causabit. Sed in illis qui nascuntur ex fornicatione, magis est vitiata origo quam in illis qui nascuntur ex legitimo matrimonio. Sequeretur ergo quod illi qui ex fornicatione nascuntur, maius peccatum contrahant nascendo; quod patet esse falsum: quia non debetur eis maior poena. [61920] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 9 Praeterea, si peccatum originale contrahitur per carnis originem, hoc non est nisi in quantum caro est corrupta. Aut ergo illa corruptio est moralis, aut naturalis. Sed moralis esse non potest: quia corruptionis moralis subiectum non est caro, sed anima. Similiter autem nec naturalis: quia sequeretur quod inficeret animam naturali actione, id est per qualitates activas et passivas; quod patet esse falsum. Nullo ergo modo peccatum contrahitur per carnis originem. [61921] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 10 Praeterea, defectus qui consecutus est ex peccato primi parentis, est carentia originalis iustitiae, ut Anselmus dicit; et sic cum originalis iustitia sit quiddam spirituale, sequitur quod defectus praedictus sit etiam spiritualis. Corruptio autem carnis est quiddam corporale. Spiritualia autem et corporalia sunt diversorum generum; et sic spirituale non potest causare effectum corporalem. Non ergo ex peccato primi parentis potuit causari corruptio in carne nostra, ex qua in nobis peccatum per originem transfunderetur. [61922] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 11 Praeterea, secundum Augustinum, peccatum originale est carentia originalis iustitiae. Aut ergo originalis iustitia conveniebat animae primi hominis naturaliter ex sua creatione, aut fuit donum superadditum ex divina liberalitate. Si autem fuit animae naturalis, nunquam eam amisisset peccando: quia, ut Dionysius dicit IV cap. de Div. Nom., data naturalia etiam in Daemonibus permanserunt; et sic etiam omnes homines originalem iustitiam haberent: quia quod est naturale uni animae, est omnibus animabus naturale; et ita nullus nasceretur cum peccato originali, idest cum carentia originalis iustitiae. Si autem fuit iustitia illa donum superadditum ex liberalitate divina: aut ergo Deus animae hominis nascentis illud donum dat, aut non. Si dat, non nascitur homo cum carentia originalis iustitiae, neque potest anima eius per carnem infici. Si autem non datur a Deo, hoc non videtur ei esse imputandum, sed Deo, qui non dedit. Nullo ergo modo homo per originem peccatum contrahere potest. [61923] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 12 Praeterea, anima rationalis non supervenit alicui formae praeexistenti: quia non adveniret materiae tamquam forma substantialis, sed tamquam materia accidentalis, quae advenit subiecto iam existenti in actu. Oportet ergo quod adveniente anima rationali, deficiant omnes formae praeexistentes, et per consequens omnia accidentia. Cessat ergo et ipsa corruptio seminis, si qua inerat a generante. Non ergo anima adveniens per carnem inquinari potest. [61924] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 13 Praeterea, motus sequitur naturam elementi praedominantis in corporibus mixtis, et per consequens omnes proprietates consequuntur illud quod praedominatur in composito. Sed anima praedominatur corpori in homine, qui ex utroque componitur; anima autem ex sua origine habet puritatem. Licet ergo caro ex sua origine aliquam impuritatem contrahat, videtur tamen quod homo nascens non debeat dici infectus peccato, sed purus. [61925] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 14 Praeterea, peccatum est cui aliqua poena debetur: sed peccato quod per originem contrahitur, non debetur aliqua poena; nam carentia visionis divinae, quae communiter assignatur ei pro poena, non videtur esse aliqua poena; quia si homo moreretur absque omni peccato, et gratiam non haberet, non posset pervenire ad visionem divinam, in qua consistit vita aeterna, secundum illud Ioan. XVII, v. 3: haec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum; et apostolus dicit, Rom. VI, 23: gratia Dei vita aeterna. Non ergo est aliquod peccatum quod per originem contrahatur. [61926] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 15 Praeterea, sicut causa prima est nobilior quam secunda, ita causa secunda est nobilior quam effectus. Sed si peccatum traducitur a primo parente, corruptio consecuta est in carne per animam primi hominis peccantis, et ex carne perducitur ad animam hominis qui nascitur ex Adam; et sic anima primi hominis est sicut causa prima, caro autem sicut causa secunda, et anima hominis generati sicut effectus ultimus. Sic ergo anima primi hominis erit nobilior, et caro nobilior quam anima hominis generati; quod est inconveniens. Non ergo peccatum potest traduci per originem. [61927] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 16 Praeterea, nihil agit nisi in quantum est actu. Sed in semine non est actu peccatum. Non ergo per semen decisum anima infici potest aliquo peccato. [61928] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 17 Praeterea, non potest esse idem causa infectionis peccati, et meriti. Sed actus generationis aliquando potest esse meritorius; puta cum aliquis in gratia existens, ad uxorem accedit causa generandae prolis, vel debiti reddendi. Non ergo ex hoc poterit causari infectio peccati in prole. [61929] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 18 Praeterea, causa particularis non inducit effectum universalem. Sed peccatum Adae fuit quoddam particulare. Non ergo potuit inficere totam humanam naturam aliquo peccato. [61930] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 19 Praeterea, dominus dicit Ezech. XVIII, v. 4: omnes animae meae sunt; et vers. 30: filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. Portaret autem, si pro peccato primi hominis hi qui ab eo nascuntur, damnarentur. Non ergo peccatum in posteros Adae traducitur propter eius peccatum. [61931] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. 1 Sed contra. Est quod dicitur, Rom. V, v. 12: per unum hominem peccatum in hunc mundum intravit. Sed non per imitationem; quia sic per Diabolum peccatum in mundum intravit, secundum illud Sap. II, 24-25: invidia Diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum. Imitantur autem illum qui sunt ex parte eius. Ergo per originem vitiatam peccatum a primo homine in posteros derivatur. [61932] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. 2 Praeterea, Augustinus dicit XIV de civitate Dei quod primus homo sponte depravatus genuit filios depravatos. Sed depravatio non fit nisi per peccatum. Ergo filii Adam ex sua origine peccatum contrahunt. [61933] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 co. Respondeo. Dicendum quod Pelagiani negaverunt aliquod peccatum per originem posse traduci. Sed hoc ex magna parte excludit necessitatem redemptionis factae per Christum, quae maxime videtur necessaria fuisse ad abolendam infectionem peccati, quae a primo parente in totam eius posteritatem derivata est, dicente apostolo, Rom. V, 18, quod sicut per unius delictum processum est in omnes homines in condemnationem, sic et per unius iustitiam in omnes homines in iustificationem vitae. Excluditur etiam necessitas pueros baptizandi, quod tamen communis Ecclesiae consuetudo habet ab apostolis derivata, ut Dionysius dicit in ecclesiastica Hierar. Et ideo simpliciter dicendum est, quod peccatum traducitur per originem a primo parente in posteros. Ad cuius evidentiam considerandum est, quod aliquis homo singularis dupliciter potest considerari: uno modo secundum quod est quaedam persona singularis; alio modo secundum quod est pars alicuius collegii, et utroque modo ad eum potest aliquis actus pertinere. Pertinet enim ad eum in quantum est singularis persona, ille actus quem proprio arbitrio et per se ipsum facit; sed in quantum est pars collegii, potest ad eum pertinere actus aliquis quem per se ipsum non facit nec proprio arbitrio, sed qui fit a toto collegio vel a pluribus de collegio vel a principe collegii; sicut illud quod princeps civitatis facit, dicitur civitas facere, ut philosophus dicit. Huiusmodi enim collegium hominum reputatur quasi unus homo, ita quod diversi homines in diversis officiis constituti sunt quasi diversa membra unius corporis naturalis, ut apostolus inducit de membris Ecclesiae, I Cor. XII, 12. Sic ergo tota multitudo hominum a primo parente humanam naturam accipientium, quasi unum collegium, vel potius sicut unum corpus unius hominis consideranda est; in qua quidem multitudo unusquisque homo, etiam ipse Adam, potest considerari vel quasi singularis persona, vel quasi aliquod membrum huius multitudinis, quae per naturalem originem derivatur ab uno. Est autem considerandum quod primo homini in sua institutione datum fuerat divinitus quoddam supernaturale donum, scilicet originalis iustitia, per quam ratio subdebatur Deo, et inferiores vires rationi, et corpus animae. Hoc autem donum non fuerat datum primo homini ut singulari personae tantum, sed ut cuidam principio totius humanae naturae, ut scilicet ab eo per originem derivaretur in posteros. Hoc autem donum acceptum primus homo per liberum arbitrium peccans amisit eo tenore quo sibi datum fuerat, scilicet pro se et pro tota sua posteritate. Defectus ergo huius doni totam eius posteritatem consequitur; et sic iste defectus eo modo traducitur in posteros quo modo traducitur humana natura; quae quidem traducitur non quidem secundum se totam, sed secundum aliquam sui partem, scilicet secundum carnem, cui Deus animam infundit; et sic sicut anima divinitus infusa pertinet ad naturam humanam ab Adam derivatam, propter carnem cui coniungitur; ita et defectus praedictus pertinet ad animam propter carnem, quae ab Adam propagatur non solum secundum corpulentam substantiam, sed etiam secundum seminalem rationem, id est non solum materialiter, sed sicut ab activo principio: sic enim filius accipit a patre naturam humanam. Si ergo consideretur iste defectus hoc modo per originem in istum hominem derivatus, secundum illud quod iste homo est quaedam persona singularis, sic huiusmodi defectus, non potest habere rationem culpae, ad cuius rationem requiritur quod sit voluntaria. Sed si consideretur iste homo generatus sicut quoddam membrum totius humanae naturae a primo parente propagatae, ac si omnes homines essent unus homo, sic habet rationem culpae propter voluntarium eius principium, quod est actuale peccatum primi parentis; sicut si dicamus, quod motus manus ad homicidium perpetrandum, secundum quod manus per se consideratur, non habet rationem culpae, quia manus de necessitate movetur ab alio. Si autem consideretur ut est pars totius hominis, qui voluntate agit, sic habet rationem culpae, quia sic est voluntarius. Sicut ergo homicidium non dicitur culpa manus, sed culpa totius hominis; ita huiusmodi defectus non dicitur esse peccatum personale, sed peccatum totius naturae; nec ad personam pertinet, nisi in quantum natura inficit personam. Et sicut ad unum peccatum faciendum diversae partes hominis adhibentur, scilicet voluntas, ratio, manus et huiusmodi, et tamen est unum solum peccatum propter unitatem principii, scilicet voluntatis, a quo peccati ratio ad omnes actus partium derivatur; ita et ratione principii in tota natura humana consideratur quasi unum peccatum originale; propter quod apostolus dicit, Rom. V, 12: in quo omnes peccaverunt; quod secundum Augustinum, potest intelligi in quo scilicet primo homine, vel in quo peccato primi hominis, ut peccatum primi hominis sit quasi commune peccatum omnium. [61934] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 1 Ad primum ergo dicendum, quod peccatum quod per originem contrahitur, dicitur voluntarium ratione sui principii, scilicet voluntatis primi parentis, ut dictum est. [61935] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 2 Ad secundum dicendum, quod istud peccatum consequitur totam naturam humanam; unde subiectum huius peccati est anima, secundum quod est pars humanae naturae: et ideo sicut humana natura traducitur, licet anima non traducatur; ita etiam peccatum originale traducitur, licet anima non traducatur. [61936] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 3 Ad tertium dicendum, quod caro non est sufficiens causa peccati actualis, sed peccati originalis est sufficiens causa; sicut et traductio carnis est sufficiens causa, materialiter tamen, humanae naturae. [61937] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 4 Ad quartum dicendum, quod ei quod est per originem contractum, non debetur poena et increpatio si referatur ad personam, quia sic non habet rationem voluntarii, sed si referatur ad naturam, sic habet rationem voluntarii, ut dictum est et hoc modo debetur ei increpatio et poena. [61938] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 5 Ad quintum dicendum, quod defectus per originem contractus habet quidem rationem existentis ab alio, si referatur ad personam, non autem si referatur ad naturam; sic enim est quasi a principio intrinseco. [61939] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 6 Ad sextum dicendum, quod caro nostra in sui natura bona est, sed secundum quod est privata originali iustitia propter peccatum primi parentis, sic causat originale peccatum. [61940] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 7 Ad septimum dicendum, quod sicut dictum est, peccatum originale per se loquendo est peccatum naturae, non personae, nisi ratione naturae infectae. Actus autem generationis proprie deservit naturae, quia ordinatur ad conservationem speciei; sed carnem iam esse animae unitam pertinet ad constitutionem personae; et ideo caro magis causat originale peccatum prout consideratur in via generationis quam prout est iam unita. [61941] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 8 Ad octavum dicendum, quod in illis qui nascuntur ex fornicatione, est quidem origo dupliciter vitiata, vitio scilicet naturae, quod traducitur ex Adam, et vitio personae, id est patris generantis, ex quo vitio nulla infectio in prole relinquitur. Quilibet enim generans traducit peccatum originale in quantum generat ut Adam, non in quantum generat ut Petrus vel Martinus; id est per id quod habet ab Adam, non per id quod est proprium sibi. [61942] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 9 Ad nonum dicendum, quod corruptio quae est in carne, est quidem actus naturalis, sed intentione et virtute moralis. Ex peccato enim primi parentis destituta est caro eius illa virtute ut ex ea possit decidi semen per quod originalis iustitia in alios propagetur; et sic in semine defectus huius virtutis est defectus moralis corruptionis, et quaedam intentio eius; sicut dicimus intentionem coloris esse in aere, et intentionem animae esse in semine. Et ex hoc etiam est ibi virtus ad similem imperfectionem, sicut est ibi virtus ad productionem humanae naturae in prole generata. [61943] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 10 Ad decimum dicendum, quod nihil prohibet a causa spirituali causari effectum corporalem. Nam et Boetius dicit in libro de Trinitate quod formae quae sunt in materia, venerunt a formis quae sunt sine materia: et in nobis ipsis a voluntate movetur inferior appetitus, ad cuius motum sequitur transmutatio corporalis. [61944] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 11 Ad undecimum dicendum, quod originalis iustitia fuit superaddita primo homini ex liberalitate divina; sed quod huic animae non detur a Deo, non est ex parte eius, sed ex parte humanae naturae, in qua invenitur contrarium prohibens. [61945] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 12 Ad duodecimum dicendum, quod in semine est corruptio originalis peccati non actu sed virtute, eo modo quo est ibi virtute humana natura: quae quidem virtus activa in semine est in spiritu spumoso, ut Aristoteles dicit in Lib. de Gener. animalium, non autem in materia quae amittit unam formam et recipit aliam. [61946] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 13 Ad decimumtertium dicendum, quod sicut Dionysius dicit IV cap. de Div. Nom., bonum contingit ex tota integra causa, sed malum provenit etiam ex singularibus defectibus; et ideo defectus qui est ex parte corporis sufficit ad integritatem humanae naturae tollendam. [61947] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 14 Ad decimumquartum dicendum, quod carentia divinae visionis dupliciter competit alicui. Uno modo sic quod non habeat in se unde possit ad divinam visionem pervenire, et sic carentia divinae visionis competeret ei qui in solis naturalibus esset etiam absque peccato; sic enim carentia divinae visionis non est poena, sed defectus consequens omnem naturam creatam: quia nulla creatura ex suis naturalibus potest pervenire ad visionem divinam. Alio modo potest alicui competere carentia divinae visionis hoc modo ut habeat in se aliquid ex quo debeatur ei quod careat visione divina; et sic carentia visionis divinae est poena et originalis et actualis peccati. [61948] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 15 Ad decimumquintum dicendum, quod duplex est causa. Una principalis quae agit per propriam formam, et haec est nobilior quam effectus in quantum est causa. Alia est causa instrumentalis quae non agit per formam propriam, sed in quantum est mota ab alio, et hanc non oportet nobiliorem esse effectu, sicut serra non est nobilior quam domus. Hoc autem modo semen carnale est causa naturae humanae in prole, et etiam culpae originalis in anima eius. [61949] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 16 Ad decimumsextum dicendum, quod aliquod agens est in actu multipliciter. Uno modo secundum propriam formam, quae vel continet formam effectus secundum similitudinem speciei, sicut ignis generat ignem; vel secundum virtutem tantum, sicut sol generat ignem. Alio modo, secundum motum ab alio; et hoc modo instrumentum agit ut ens actu: et sic etiam semen est actu, in quantum est in eo motus et intentio animae generantis, secundum philosophum in Lib. de Gener. animalium; et ex hoc habet virtutem causandi et humanam naturam et originale peccatum. [61950] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 17 Ad decimumseptimum dicendum, quod aliquis vir iustus accedendo ad uxorem meretur secundum id quod est proprium sibi; et sic non transmittit peccatum originale, sed secundum id quod habet ab Adam, ut supra dictum est. [61951] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 18 Ad decimumoctavum dicendum, quod Adam in quantum fuit principium humanae naturae, habuit rationem causae universalis, et ita per eius actum corrupta est tota humana natura, quae ab eo propagatur. [61952] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 19 Ad decimumnonum dicendum, quod peccatum primi hominis est quodammodo peccatum commune totius humanae naturae, ut dictum est; et ideo cum aliquis punitur pro peccato primi parentis, non punitur pro peccato alterius, sed pro peccato suo.

[61911] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 tit. 2 And it seems not.

[61912] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 1 For it is called Ecclesi. 15, 18: before man life and death, good and evil: whatsoever he will, it shall be given him. From this it may be understood that sin, which is the spiritual death of the soul, consists in the will. But nothing that man contracts from his origin consists in his will. Therefore man contracts no sin from his origin.

[61913] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 2 Further, an accident is not translated except by the translation of its subject. But the subject of sin is the rational soul. Since, then, the rational soul is not translated by origin, as we find in Lib. of Eccl. dogmas, it seems that no sin is contracted by origin.

[61914] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 3 But it must be said that although the subject of sin is not translated, the flesh is nevertheless translated, which is the cause of sin. because when they are placed, no effect is placed. But the flesh is not a sufficient cause of sin; for no matter how much the flesh entices to sin, it is still in the power of the will to consent or not to consent; and thus the will itself is a sufficient cause of sin. But the will is not translated. Therefore the transfer of the flesh is not sufficient for the transfer of any sin.

[61915] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 4 Further, sin, as it is now accepted, is to whom punishment and rebuke are due. But no rebuke and punishment is due to any defect contracted from the origin: for as the Philosopher says in Ethic. but he is reprimanded if he is blind from drunkenness. Therefore no defect which is contracted from the origin has the character of sin.

[61916] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 5 Further, Augustine distinguishes two kinds of evil in 1 On free will: one that we do, which is the evil of guilt, and another that we suffer, which belongs to the evil of punishment. But every deficiency which is from another has the aspect of suffering; for passion is the effect and inference of action. Therefore nothing contracted by origin from another has the character of sin, but only the character of punishment.

[61917] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 6 Further, in Lib. It is said of ecclesiastical dogmas: Our flesh is good, since it was created by a good God. But good is not the cause of evil, according to Matt. 7, 18: a tree cannot produce good fruit that is bad. Therefore original sin is not contracted through the origin of the flesh.

[61918] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 7 Further, the soul depends more on the flesh after it is united to it than on its union itself. But after the soul is already united to the flesh, it cannot be infected by the flesh except by its consent. Therefore, neither in the union itself. Therefore original sin cannot be contracted through the origin of the flesh.

[61919] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Objection 8. Further, if a vitiated origin of the flesh causes sin in the soul, the more vitiated by its origin, the greater the sin it will cause. But in those who are born of fornication, the origin is more defective than in those who are born of legitimate marriage. It would therefore follow that those who are born from fornication contract a greater sin by being born; which is evidently false: because no greater punishment is due to them.

[61920] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, if original sin is contracted through the origin of the flesh, this is only in so far as the flesh is corrupted. Then that corruption is either moral or natural. But it cannot be moral: because the subject of moral corruption is not the flesh, but the soul. Similarly, neither is the natural: because it follows that it infects the soul with natural activity, that is, through active and passive qualities; which is clearly false. In no way, therefore, is sin contracted through the origin of the flesh.

[61921] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 10 Further, the defect which resulted from the sin of the first parent is the lack of original justice, as Anselm says; and so since the original justice is something spiritual, it follows that the aforesaid deficiency is also spiritual. But the corruption of the flesh is something corporeal. But the spiritual and the corporeal are of different kinds; and thus the spiritual cannot cause a bodily effect. Therefore, the corruption in our flesh could not have been caused by the sin of the first parent, from which sin was transfused into us through the origin.

[61922] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, according to Augustine, original sin is the lack of original justice. Either then the original justice belonged to the soul of the first man naturally from his own creation, or it was an added gift from divine liberality. But if it had been a natural soul, it would never have lost it by sinning: because, as Dionysius says, chapter 4. of Div. Nom., natural data also remained in the demons; and thus also all men would have original justice: because what is natural to one soul is natural to all souls; and thus no one would be born with original sin, that is, with a lack of original righteousness. But if that justice was a gift added from divine liberality: then either God gives that gift to the soul of man being born, or not. If he gives, man is not born with a lack of original justice, nor can his soul be infected by the flesh. But if it is not given by God, this does not seem to be imputed to him, but to God, who did not give. In no way, therefore, can man contract original sin.

[61923] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 12 Further, the rational soul does not come upon any pre-existing form: because it does not come to matter as a substantial form, but as accidental matter, which comes to a subject already existing in act. It is necessary, therefore, that when the rational soul arrives, all pre-existing forms should fail, and consequently all accidents. Therefore the corruption of the seed also ceases, if it was inherent in the progenitor. Therefore the coming soul cannot be defiled by the flesh.

[61924] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 13 Further, motion follows the nature of the predominant element in mixed bodies, and consequently all the properties result from that which predominates in the compound. But the soul predominates over the body in man, which is composed of both; but the soul has purity from its origin. Although, therefore, the flesh has contracted some impurity from its origin, it seems that a person who is born should not be said to be infected with sin, but pure.

[61925] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 14. Further, there is a sin to which some punishment is due: but a sin which is contracted through the origin, no punishment is due; for the lack of divine vision, which is commonly assigned to him as a punishment, does not seem to be any kind of punishment; because if a man died without all sin, and had no grace, he would not be able to reach the divine vision, in which eternal life consists, according to John 17, v. 3: this is eternal life, that they may know you alone as the true God; and the Apostle says, Rom. 6, 23: eternal life by the grace of God. Therefore there is no sin which is contracted by origin.

[61926] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, just as the first cause is more noble than the second, so the second cause is more noble than the effect. But if sin is transmitted from the first parent, corruption has followed in the flesh through the soul of the first man who sinned, and it is brought from the flesh to the soul of the man who is born from Adam; and thus the soul of the first man is like the first cause, and the flesh like the second cause, and the soul of the man begotten like the last effect. Thus, then, the soul of the first man will be more noble, and the flesh more noble than the soul of the first man; which is inappropriate. Therefore, sin cannot be transmitted by origin.

[61927] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 16 Further, he does nothing except in so far as he actually is. But there is no actual sin in the seed. Therefore, the soul cannot be infected with any sin through the seed that has been cut.

[61928] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 17 Further, the cause of the infection of sin and merit cannot be the same. But the act of generation can sometimes be meritorious; for example, when a man existing in grace goes to his wife for the purpose of begetting children, or to repay a debt. Therefore the infection of sin in the offspring cannot be caused from this.

[61929] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 18 Further, a particular cause does not bring about a universal effect. But Adam's sin was a particular one. Therefore he could not infect the whole human nature with any sin.

[61930] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 19 Further, the Lord says Ezek. 18, v. 4: All souls are mine; and verse 30: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. But it would bear, if for the sin of the first man those who are born from him were condemned. Therefore sin is not transferred to Adam's descendants because of her sin.

[61931] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. 1 Sed contra. Est quod dicitur, Rom. V, v. 12: through one man sin entered into this world. Sed non per imitationem; because thus sin entered the world through the Devil, according to Wisdom. II, 24-25: the envy of the Devil, death entered the world. Let those who are from his side imitate him. Therefore, through a vitiated origin, sin is derived from the first man to posterity.

[61932] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. Objection 2. Further, Augustine says in Chapter 14 of the City of God that the first man, being depraved of his own accord, begat depraved children. But perversion does not take place except through sin. Therefore the children of Adam contract sin from their origin.

[61933] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 co. I answer It must be said that the Pelagians denied that any sin could be transmitted through origin. But this to a great extent excludes the necessity of the redemption effected by Christ, which seems to have been most necessary to abolish the infection of sin, which was derived from the first parent into all his posterity, as the apostle says, Rom. 5:18, that just as by the offense of one there is a process on all men to condemnation, so also by the righteousness of one on all men to the justification of life. The necessity of baptizing children is also excluded, which is nevertheless a common custom of the Church derived from the apostles, as Dionysius says in the Ecclesiastical Hierar. And therefore it must be said simply that sin is transmitted by origin from the first parent to the posterity. For the evidence of which we must consider that a singular person can be considered in two ways: in the first way, according to the fact that he is a certain singular person; in another way, according to the fact that it is a part of some college, and in both ways an act may belong to it. For it belongs to him in so far as he is a singular person, that act which he does of his own free will and by himself; but in so far as he is a part of the college, any act which he does not do by himself or of his own free will, but which is done by the whole college, or by several of the college, or by the leader of the college, may belong to him. just as what the ruler of the state does, the state is said to do, as the philosopher says. For such a college of men is regarded as one man, so that different men are appointed to different offices as if they were different members of one natural body, as the Apostle says about the members of the Church, 1 Cor. 12, 12. Thus, therefore, the whole multitude of men who receive human nature from their first parent, is to be considered as one college, or rather as one body of one man; in which multitude each man, even Adam himself, may be considered either as a singular person, or as some member of this multitude, which is derived by natural origin from one. Now it must be considered that the first man, in his institution, had been divinely given a certain supernatural gift, namely, original justice, by which reason was subject to God, and the lower powers of reason, and the body of the soul. Now this gift had not been given to the first man as a singular person only, but as a certain principle of the whole human nature, namely, that it should be derived from him through the origin to posterity. But this gift received by the first man, by sinning through his free will, he lost in the manner in which it had been given to him, that is, for himself and for all his posterity. Therefore, the failure of this gift affects all his posterity; and thus this defect is transmitted to posterity in the same way as human nature is transmitted; which indeed is translated not according to itself as a whole, but according to some part of itself, that is, according to the flesh, into which God infuses the soul; and thus, just as the divinely infused soul belongs to the human nature derived from Adam, because of the flesh to which it is united; so also the aforesaid defect pertains to the soul because of the flesh, which is propagated from Adam not only according to the corpulent substance, but also according to the seminal reason, that is, not only materially, but as from an active principle: for thus the son receives from the father the human nature. If, therefore, this defect is considered to have been derived in this way by origin in that man, according to the fact that this man is a kind of singular person, then this kind of defect cannot have the character of guilt, for the character of which it is required that it be voluntary. But if this man begotten be considered as a certain member of the whole human nature propagated by the first parent, as if all men were one man, then he has the reason of guilt because of his voluntary principle, which is the actual sin of the first parent. as if we were to say that the movement of the hand to commit murder, according as the hand is considered by itself, has no reason for guilt, because the hand is necessarily moved by another. But if it be considered that he is a part of the whole man, who acts by his will, he has the reason of guilt, because he is thus voluntary. Just as, then, murder is not called the fault of the hand, but the fault of the whole man; Thus a deficiency of this kind is not said to be a personal sin, but a sin of the whole nature. nor does it pertain to the person, except in so far as nature infects the person. And just as different parts of man are used to commit one sin, namely the will, the reason, the hands, and the like, and yet there is only one sin because of the unity of the principle, namely the will, from which the reason for sin is derived for all the acts of the parts. so also by reason of the principle in all human nature it is considered as one original sin; propter quod apostolus dicit, Rom. V, 12: in quo omnes peccaverunt; which, according to Augustine, can be understood in which namely the first man, or in which sin of the first man, so that the sin of the first man is as it were the common sin of all.

[61934] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 1 To the first reply, therefore, that a sin which is contracted by origin is said to be voluntary by reason of its principle, namely, the will of the first parent, as has been said.

[61935] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 2 To the second reply, that this sin follows the whole human nature; whence the subject of this sin is the soul, inasmuch as it is a part of human nature: and therefore as human nature is transgressed, although the soul is not transgressed; so even original sin is transferred, although the soul is not transferred.

[61936] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 3 Reply to Objection 3: The flesh is not a sufficient cause of actual sin, but it is a sufficient cause of original sin. just as the transmigration of the flesh is a sufficient cause, however materially, of human nature.

[61937] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 4 Reply to the fourth, that what is contracted by origin is not due punishment and rebuke if it is referred to a person, because in this way it does not have the aspect of the will, but if it is related to nature, it has the aspect of the will, as has been said, and in this way rebuke and punishment are due to it.

[61938] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 5. To the fifth answer, that a deficiency by the origin of a contract indeed has the aspect of existing from another, if it is referred to a person, but not if it is referred to a nature. for it is so, as it were, from an intrinsic principle.

[61939] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 6. To the sixth answer, that our flesh is good in its own nature, but inasmuch as it is deprived of original justice because of the sin of the first parent, so it causes original sin.

[61940] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 7. To the seventh answer, that, as has been said, original sin, speaking in itself, is a sin of the nature, not of the person, but by reason of the infected nature. Now the act of generation properly serves nature, because it is directed to the preservation of the species; but the fact that the flesh is already united to the soul belongs to the constitution of the person; and therefore the flesh causes original sin more as it is considered in the way of generation than as it is already united.

[61941] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 8. To the eighth answer, that in those who are born of fornication, it is indeed twofold in origin, viz., the vice of nature, which is transmitted from Adam, and the vice of the person, that is, the begetting father, from which vice no infection is left in the offspring. For everyone who begets transmits original sin to the extent that he generates like Adam, not to the extent that he generates like Peter or Martin; that is by what he has from Adam, not by what is proper to him.

[61942] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 9. To the ninth answer, that the corruption which is in the flesh is indeed a natural act, but by intention and moral virtue. For from the sin of the first parent his flesh was deprived of that virtue, so that from it the seed may be dropped by which the original righteousness is propagated to others; and thus in the seed the lack of this virtue is the lack of moral corruption, and a kind of intention thereof; as we say that the concentration of color is in the air, and the concentration of the soul is in the seed. And from this also there is virtue for a similar imperfection, just as there is virtue for the production of human nature in offspring.

[61943] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 10. To answer the tenth, that nothing prevents a spiritual cause from causing a corporeal effect. For Boethius also says in his book on the Trinity that the forms which are in matter came from the forms which are without matter: and in us the lower appetite is moved by the will, to the movement of which bodily transformation follows.

[61944] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 11 Regarding the eleventh answer, that the original justice was added to the first man out of divine liberality; but what is not given to this soul by God is not on his part, but on the part of human nature, in which the contrary is found preventing.

[61945] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 12. Regarding the twelfth answer, that the corruption of original sin is in the seed, not actually but by virtue, in the same way that human nature is there by virtue: which virtue is active in the seed in the foaming spirit, as Aristotle says in Lib. of Gen. of animals, but not in matter which loses one form and receives another.

[61946] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 13 Regarding the thirteenth point, as Dionysius says in chapter 4. of Div. Nom., good occurs from a whole whole cause, but evil also results from individual defects; and therefore the deficiency which is in the part of the body is sufficient to take away the integrity of human nature.

[61947] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 14. To the fourteenth answer, that the lack of divine vision befits a person in two ways. On the one hand, this is because he does not have in himself the means by which he can reach the divine vision, and thus the lack of divine vision would belong to him who was in the natural sun even without sin. for thus the lack of the divine vision is not a punishment, but a deficiency consequent upon all created nature: for no creature of its natural nature can attain to the divine vision. In another way, the lack of divine vision may belong to someone in this way, that he has something in himself from which it is due to him that he lacks divine vision; and thus the lack of divine vision is the punishment of both original and actual sin.

[61948] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 15 The fifteenth point is that the cause is twofold. One of the principal things that acts through its own form, and this is more noble than the effect in so far as it is the cause. There is another instrumental cause which does not act through its own form, but in so far as it is moved by another, and this need not be more noble in its effect, just as a saw is not more noble than a house. But in this way the carnal seed is the cause of the human nature in the offspring, and also of the original guilt in his soul.

[61949] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 16 To answer the sixteenth, that any agent is in act in many ways. In the first way, according to the proper form, which either contains the form of the effect according to the likeness of the species, just as fire begets fire; or according to power only, as the sun generates fire. In another way, according to motion from another; and in this way the instrument acts as an actual being: and so also the seed is actually, in so far as there is in it the movement and intention of the generative soul, according to the philosopher in Lib. of Gen. of animals; and from this he has the power of causing both human nature and original sin.

[61950] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 17 To the seventeenth answer, that a man, by approaching his wife justly, deserves according to what is proper to him; and so he does not transmit original sin, but according to what he has from Adam, as was said above.

[61951] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 18. To answer the eighteenth, that Adam, in so far as he was the principle of human nature, had the idea of a universal cause, and thus by his act the whole of human nature, which is propagated by him, was corrupted.

[61952] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 19 To answer the nineteenth, that the sin of the first man is in a way the common sin of the whole human nature, as has been said; and therefore when a man is punished for the sin of his first parent, he is not punished for the sin of another, but for his own sin.
